Walter Gropius. From 1883 to 1969, a German architect and educator who founded and directed the Bauhaus, the most influential art and design school of the twentieth century. His vision of uniting art, craft, and industry through systematic design education revolutionized architectural practice and design philosophy, establishing principles of functionalism and modernism that shaped contemporary aesthetics and the built environment worldwide.

Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar, Germany in 1919, an experimental school integrating fine art, craft, architecture, and industrial design under one pedagogical umbrella with the motto form follows function. The Bauhaus taught that good design should be democratic, accessible, and honest to materials. Beauty emerged from utility and rational structure, not ornament, a radical break from Art Nouveau and historicism. Gropius assembled a faculty of modernist luminaries including Wassily Kandinsky, Paul Klee, and László Moholy-Nagy, who taught students that art was not separate from everyday life but essential to it.

Gropius advocated functionalism in architecture. Buildings should express their purpose through clear, undecorated form. Structure and utility determine aesthetic, and materials like steel, glass, and concrete should be honestly expressed. As an architect, he designed the Bauhaus school building itself from 1925 to 1926 in Dessau, a masterpiece of modernist principle featuring clean lines, geometric volumes, extensive glazing, and functional transparency.

The Bauhaus was suppressed by the Nazi regime in 1933. Nazis despised modernism as degenerate. Gropius emigrated to the United States, where he taught at Harvard and influenced American modernist architecture. His legacy extends through generations of architects and designers who learned Bauhaus principles. His integration of art, industry, and education remains foundational to contemporary design education.
